newsitem.title: UK: JOBS-European jobless totals seen easing by 1998.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-European jobless totals seen easing by 1998.

text.p: European unemployment is expected to fall over the next two years as governments move beyond the initial constraints of meeting stringent targets for currency union, and growth picks up, according to forecasts compiled by Reuters.

Figures collected in January for a Reuters survey for the Group of Seven developed countries show that unemployment in Europe and Canada is expected to fall by the second half of 1998, while in the United States and Japan jobless rates are expected to remain steady.
Unemployment data for France and Germany released since then have prompted many economists to revise up predictions for these countries, but their overall forecast for Europe remains the same.

Tight fiscal policy designed to reduce budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, in order to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, is expected to some extent to be loosened, analysts said.
This would support growth in most of Europe, analysts said.
"There is a reasonably healthy economic recovery under way in Europe. Exceptions are Germany and France," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Europe, in London.
French unemployment was at a record 12.7 percent in January, while German unemployment, at 11.3 percent in January, is at a post-war high.
In both countries stagnant growth and failure to reform the labour market are given as reasons for revisions.
According to the numbers collected by Reuters from economists and forecasters across the G7, French unemployment is expected to fall, but not significantly.

"Significant falls in unemployment will require structural reforms of the labour market. There has been some, but it will only have an effect in the longer term," said David Naude, senior economist for France at JP Morgan in Paris.
Italian unemployment is forecast to fall to 11.4 percent by third quarter 1998 from 12.2 percent in October 1996.

"We expect a slight increase this year because growth will be low and public finances will be hit by trying to meet EMU criteria. But next year we should see growth gather steam," said Marcello Esposito, economist at Banca Commerciale Italiana in Milan.
In Britain, analysts expect unemployment to keep falling. The average of forecasts in the January survey for third quarter 1998 is six percent from 6.5 percent in January.
"Britain's government has not been restricted by trying to meet the Maastricht criteria," said a UK analyst.
"Labour market reforms started in the last decade have given Britain one of the most flexible workforces in Europe."
Britain is almost certain to stay on the sidelines when European Union partners launch the single currency in 1999.
HOW DO JAPAN, NORTH AMERICA COMPARE?

In Japan unemployment rates are forecast to remain at over three percent for the next two years, the survey which collected G7 forecasts throughout January, showed. Analysts are not changing their numbers, but are sceptical about how unemployment is defined in Japan.
"Nobody in their right minds believes unemployment is that low. The policy of 'make-work', where there are two or three people doing one person's job, distorts the picture" said Jessop.

Canada is the only G7 country expected to make significant gains in employment. The average of forecasts from the survey shows unemployment at 8.9 percent by third quarter 1998 from 9.7 percent in January.

"Canada has been the poor man of the G7 for a while. It's catching up in terms of growth and liberalisation. This combined with low interest rates will fuel the economy," said a North American analyst.
"To date, growth has been export-led and a pick-up in the domestic economy is needed to ensure lower unemployment. I believe the fundamental building blocks are now in place."
Unemployment in the United States is forecast at 5.5 percent by end-1998, slightly higher than the 5.4 percent seen in January.
